concepts.title: Iterators and Generators
concepts.description: Every for loop runs on the iterator protocol under the hood, and generator functions use yield to pause and resume execution, producing values lazily instead of building a whole collection in memory up front.
learningObjectives: Explain the iterator protocol (__iter__, __next__, StopIteration) and what a for loop actually does under the hood.
Write a generator function using yield and explain how it pauses and resumes state between calls.
Contrast a generator function's execution model with a regular function that runs top to bottom on every call.
Explain the memory and laziness tradeoff between a generator expression and a list comprehension.
Identify a real scenario (like processing a huge file) where a generator is clearly the right choice over building a full list.

sections.heading: What a for Loop Actually Does: The Iterator Protocol
sections.body:
`for item in some_list:` looks like a single, atomic operation, but it's actually built entirely out of two more primitive pieces that any object can implement: the **iterable** protocol and the **iterator** protocol.

An **iterable** is anything with an `__iter__` method, which returns an **iterator**. An **iterator** is an object with a `__next__` method, which returns the next value each time it's called, and raises the built-in `StopIteration` exception once there's nothing left to produce. A `for` loop is syntactic sugar for calling `iter()` once (which calls `__iter__` under the hood) and then calling `next()` repeatedly (which calls `__next__`) until `StopIteration` is raised, at which point the loop ends cleanly -- you never see that exception yourself because the `for` loop catches it for you:

```python
numbers = [10, 20, 30]

# what 'for n in numbers:' does, spelled out manually:
iterator = iter(numbers)
while True:
    try:
        n = next(iterator)
    except StopIteration:
        break
    print(n)
# prints 10, 20, 30
```

This matters because it explains *why* so many different things -- lists, strings, dicts, files, ranges, sets, and your own custom classes -- can all be looped over with the exact same `for` syntax: none of them need to be a 'list-like' thing at all, they just need to cooperate with this two-method protocol. A list is iterable, but a list itself is *not* its own iterator -- calling `iter([1,2,3])` produces a separate, fresh list-iterator object each time, which is why you can have two independent `for` loops over the same list running conceptually 'at the same time' without interfering with each other.

sections.heading: yield: Functions That Pause and Resume
sections.body:
A regular function runs from its first line to a `return` (or the end of its body) in one uninterrupted pass, every single time it's called -- its local state is created fresh on entry and discarded entirely on exit. A **generator function** looks almost identical, but contains at least one `yield` statement instead of (or alongside) `return`, and that one keyword changes its entire execution model.

Calling a generator function does not run any of its code immediately -- it returns a **generator object** (which is both an iterable and its own iterator) without executing a single line of the body yet. Each call to `next()` on that generator object runs the function's code **up to the next `yield`**, hands back the yielded value, and then -- critically -- **pauses execution right there**, preserving every local variable and its exact position in the code. The *next* call to `next()` resumes exactly where it left off, rather than starting over:

```python
def count_up_to(n):
    print("starting")
    i = 1
    while i <= n:
        print(f"about to yield {i}")
        yield i
        print(f"resumed after yielding {i}")
        i += 1
    print("done")

gen = count_up_to(3)   # nothing printed yet -- no code has run
print(next(gen))       # 'starting', 'about to yield 1', then returns 1
print(next(gen))       # 'resumed after yielding 1', 'about to yield 2', then returns 2
print(next(gen))       # 'resumed after yielding 2', 'about to yield 3', then returns 3
# a further next(gen) would print 'resumed after yielding 3', 'done', then raise StopIteration
```

Notice that `"starting"` doesn't print until the *first* `next()` call, not when `count_up_to(3)` itself is called -- creating the generator object does no work at all. And `i`'s value is genuinely remembered between calls, along with the exact line execution paused on -- this is a fundamentally different execution model from an ordinary function, which has no concept of 'pausing' at all.

sections.heading: Generator Expressions vs List Comprehensions: The Laziness Tradeoff
sections.body:
A **generator expression** looks almost identical to a list comprehension, but with parentheses instead of square brackets: `(x * 2 for x in range(1000000))` instead of `[x * 2 for x in range(1000000)]`. The syntactic similarity hides a significant difference in behavior. A list comprehension builds the **entire** list in memory immediately, all at once. A generator expression builds **nothing** up front -- it creates a generator object that computes each value lazily, one at a time, only when something actually asks for the next one (via a `for` loop, `next()`, or being passed to something like `sum()` or `list()`).

```python
squares_list = [x * x for x in range(1_000_000)]      # allocates a full list of a million ints, right now
squares_gen = (x * x for x in range(1_000_000))         # allocates almost nothing yet

print(sum(squares_list))   # works, but the whole list existed in memory the whole time
print(sum(squares_gen))    # works too, computing and discarding one value at a time
```

Both ultimately produce the same sum, but `squares_list` requires memory proportional to a million integers, held all at once, while `squares_gen` never holds more than one value at a time in memory. This is the fundamental tradeoff: a list comprehension is the right choice when you actually need the whole collection available -- to index into it, iterate over it multiple times, or pass it somewhere that specifically expects a list. A generator is the right choice when you're going to consume the values exactly once, in order, and don't need random access -- you trade the ability to re-iterate or index for a dramatically smaller memory footprint, which matters enormously once the sequence is large or, as below, unbounded.

sections.heading: Where This Actually Matters: Processing a Huge File Line by Line
sections.body:
The abstract memory argument becomes concrete with a realistic example: searching a multi-gigabyte log file for lines containing an error:

```python
def find_errors(filename):
    with open(filename, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:              # a file object is itself a lazy line-by-line iterator
            if "ERROR" in line:
                yield line.rstrip("\n")

for error_line in find_errors("huge_app.log"):
    print(error_line)
```

Iterating over an open file object with `for line in f:` never loads the whole file into memory -- it reads and yields one line at a time, which is exactly why files are iterable in the first place. `find_errors` is a generator function layered on top of that: it filters lazily, yielding only matching lines, one at a time, as the caller asks for them. Compare this to the tempting-but-wrong alternative, `return [line for line in f if "ERROR" in line]`, which would read the *entire* file into memory as a list before returning anything at all -- fine for a small file, but potentially catastrophic (or simply impossible) for a file that's larger than available RAM. The generator version can process a file of effectively any size using a small, constant amount of memory, and -- as a bonus -- the caller starts seeing matching lines immediately, without waiting for the entire file to be scanned first.

examples.title: The for Loop, Spelled Out Manually
examples.explanation: CountdownIterator implements both halves of the protocol: __iter__ (returning itself, since it's already an iterator) and __next__ (producing the next value, or raising StopIteration once exhausted). The for loop calls iter() once, getting back the object itself, and then calls next() repeatedly -- 3, then 2, then 1 -- until __next__ raises StopIteration on the fourth call, which the for loop silently catches to end the loop. This is exactly the mechanism every built-in iterable (lists, ranges, files, dict views) relies on; writing your own class that implements __iter__ and __next__ makes it usable in a for loop, in list(), in sum(), and everywhere else Python expects an iterable, with no special-casing needed anywhere.

examples.title: A Generator Function Pausing and Resuming
examples.code:
def fibonacci_up_to(limit):
    a, b = 0, 1
    while a <= limit:
        yield a
        a, b = b, a + b

for num in fibonacci_up_to(20):
    print(num, end=" ")
# 0 1 1 2 3 5 8 13

# Turning it into a list explicitly, if you actually need one:
all_values = list(fibonacci_up_to(20))
print(all_values)   # [0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13]
examples.explanation: fibonacci_up_to is a generator function -- calling it returns a generator object immediately, without computing anything. Each time the for loop asks for the next value, execution resumes right after the previous yield, with a and b holding exactly the values they had when execution paused, computes the next Fibonacci number, and yields it, pausing again. The while loop's condition (a <= limit) is re-checked each time execution resumes, and once it's false, the generator function simply finishes running (falls off the end), which raises StopIteration automatically -- ending the for loop. list(fibonacci_up_to(20)) shows that a generator can always be converted into a full list on demand by consuming it entirely -- but doing so gives up the laziness/memory benefit, so it should only be done when you genuinely need random access or repeated iteration over all the values.

examples.title: List Comprehension vs Generator Expression: Same Values, Different Memory Behavior
examples.code:
import sys

squares_list = [x * x for x in range(100_000)]
squares_gen = (x * x for x in range(100_000))

print(sys.getsizeof(squares_list))   # a real number of bytes proportional to 100,000 ints
print(sys.getsizeof(squares_gen))    # a small, fixed number of bytes -- same regardless of range size

print(sum(squares_list))   # 333328333350000
print(sum(squares_gen))    # 333328333350000  -- identical result, computed lazily
examples.explanation: sys.getsizeof reveals the core difference directly: squares_list has already materialized 100,000 integers into an actual list object in memory, so its size scales with the range; squares_gen is a small object that holds only the loop's current state (the underlying range iterator and the expression to apply), and its reported size would be virtually identical even if range(100_000) were range(100_000_000) instead. Both sum() calls produce the exact same total -- consuming a generator is functionally equivalent to consuming a list, one value at a time -- but sum(squares_gen) never holds more than the current x*x in memory, computing, summing, and discarding each value as it goes.

misconceptions.description: A generator expression like (x*x for x in range(1000000)) still builds the whole sequence of a million values immediately -- it's basically just a list comprehension with different-looking syntax.
misconceptions.clarification: A generator expression builds nothing at all up front. It creates a lightweight generator object that computes each value lazily, one at a time, only when something actually requests the next one -- via a for loop, next(), or being consumed by a function like sum() or list(). This is the entire reason generator expressions exist as a distinct feature from list comprehensions: they trade the ability to index into the result or iterate over it more than once for a dramatically smaller, constant memory footprint, since at most one element's worth of computation needs to exist in memory at any given moment.

misconceptions.description: Calling a generator function runs its code the same way calling a regular function does -- the difference is just that yield lets it return multiple values instead of one.
misconceptions.clarification: Calling a generator function does not execute any of its code at all -- it immediately returns a generator object, with the function body still entirely unrun. Code inside only executes when something calls next() on that generator (directly, or via a for loop), and even then, only up to the next yield statement, at which point execution genuinely pauses -- preserving local variables and the exact position in the code -- until the next next() call resumes it. This pause-and-resume model has no equivalent in ordinary functions, which always run their entire body, top to bottom, in one uninterrupted pass, every single time they're called.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and in what order?
exercises.code:
def lazy_numbers():
    print("A")
    yield 1
    print("B")
    yield 2
    print("C")

gen = lazy_numbers()
print("created generator")
print(next(gen))
print(next(gen))
hints: Calling lazy_numbers() itself doesn't run any code inside the function -- when does the first print('A') actually happen?
Each next(gen) call resumes execution right where the PREVIOUS yield left off, runs until the NEXT yield (or the end), and returns whatever's yielded.
Walk through it call by call: what runs (and prints) between 'created generator' and the first next() returning, and then between the first and second next()?
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'created generator', then 'A', then '1' (the returned value), then 'B', then '2'. lazy_numbers() itself runs no code; the first next(gen) runs up to the first yield (printing 'A', returning 1); the second next(gen) resumes after that yield, prints 'B', and returns 2 at the second yield.
exercises.solutionExplanation: gen = lazy_numbers() creates a generator object without executing a single line of the function body -- that's why 'created generator' prints before anything from inside lazy_numbers. The first next(gen) call starts execution from the top: it prints 'A', then hits `yield 1`, which pauses execution and hands back 1 -- so print(next(gen)) prints '1'. The second next(gen) call resumes exactly after that yield: it prints 'B', then hits `yield 2`, pausing again and returning 2, so print(next(gen)) prints '2'. Note that 'C' never prints in this exercise, since a third next(gen) call (which would resume after yield 2, print 'C', and then raise StopIteration on hitting the end of the function) is never made.

exercises.prompt: Write a generator function `batched(iterable, size)` that takes any iterable and a batch size, and yields successive lists (batches) of up to `size` items at a time, lazily -- it should not build the whole input into memory first. For example, list(batched(range(7), 3)) should be [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6]] (the last batch may be smaller than size).
hints: You'll need to pull items from the iterable one at a time (an ordinary for loop over it works fine) and accumulate them into a temporary list until it reaches size.
Once your temporary batch list reaches `size` items, yield it, and then start a fresh, empty list for the next batch.
Don't forget the final, possibly-shorter batch: after the loop ends, if there's a partially-filled batch left over that was never yielded, yield it too.
exercises.solutionCode:
def batched(iterable, size):
    batch = []
    for item in iterable:
        batch.append(item)
        if len(batch) == size:
            yield batch
            batch = []
    if batch:              # leftover partial batch at the end
        yield batch

print(list(batched(range(7), 3)))   # [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6]]
print(list(batched("abcdef", 2)))   # [['a', 'b'], ['c', 'd'], ['e', 'f']]
exercises.solutionExplanation: batched accumulates items from the input iterable into a local list, batch, one at a time via an ordinary for loop -- this works over any iterable (a range, a string, a list, even another generator) without requiring random access or knowing its length in advance. Once batch reaches the requested size, it's yielded (handing that batch to whoever is consuming the generator) and then reset to a fresh empty list so the next batch starts clean -- reusing the same list object after yielding it would be a bug, since the caller might still be holding a reference to the batch that was just yielded. After the for loop finishes, there may be a partial batch left over (fewer than size items, from the tail of the iterable) that was never yielded inside the loop -- the final `if batch:` check yields that leftover batch too, but only if it's non-empty, which correctly handles inputs whose length is an exact multiple of size (no leftover batch to yield) as well as inputs that leave a remainder.

assessments.prompt: What actually happens when you call a generator function, like calling gen = my_generator_function(10)?
options: The function body runs immediately, top to bottom, and gen ends up holding whatever the last yield produced.
The function body runs immediately up to (and including) the first yield, and gen holds that first yielded value.
No code in the function body runs yet; gen is a generator object, and code only starts executing once next() is called on it.
Python raises a TypeError, because functions containing yield cannot be called directly -- they must be used only in a for loop.
assessments.explanation: Calling a generator function never executes any of its body immediately -- it returns a generator object right away, with execution not yet started. Code inside only begins running (up to the first yield) on the first call to next() (which a for loop performs automatically under the hood). Option A and B both incorrectly assume some code runs at call time. Option D is wrong -- calling a generator function directly is completely legal and is exactly how you obtain the generator object in the first place; a for loop is simply a convenient way to repeatedly call next() on it for you.

assessments.prompt: You need to find and process the first line containing a specific keyword in a 40 GB log file, then stop. Which approach is most appropriate, and why?
options: Read the whole file into one big string with f.read(), then split it into lines and search that list -- simplest to write.
Use `for line in f:` to iterate the open file object lazily, checking each line and breaking as soon as a match is found.
Use a list comprehension, [line for line in f if keyword in line], and take the first element of the resulting list.
Load the file with f.readlines() into a list of lines, then loop over that list with a for loop.
assessments.explanation: Option B is the only approach that never requires the full 40 GB file to exist in memory at once -- iterating an open file object with a for loop reads and yields one line at a time, lazily, and break stops iteration (and further reading) the moment a match is found, without touching the rest of the file at all. Options A, C, and D all force the entire file into memory first (as one giant string, a full list via the comprehension, or a full list via readlines()) before any searching or stopping can happen -- wasteful and potentially impossible for a file this large, especially when you only need the very first match.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to someone who understands regular functions but has never seen yield before, what makes a generator function fundamentally different from a regular function -- not just in syntax, but in execution model.
assessments.modelAnswer: A regular function, once called, runs from its first line straight through to a return statement or the end of its body, in one single, uninterrupted pass -- every call starts fresh, and once the function returns, all of its local state is gone. A generator function -- any function containing at least one yield statement -- behaves completely differently. Calling it doesn't run any of its code at all; it immediately hands back a generator object, an iterator that remembers where execution should begin. Only when something calls next() on that generator object does any code actually run, and even then, only up to the next yield statement: at that point execution genuinely pauses, mid-function, with every local variable's current value and the exact line of code preserved -- not discarded the way a regular function's locals are on return. The next call to next() doesn't restart the function from the top; it resumes execution from exactly that paused point, continuing until it hits another yield (pausing again) or reaches the end of the function body (which raises StopIteration automatically, signaling there's nothing left). This pause-and-resume model is what makes generators fundamentally different from 'a function that can return multiple things' -- they maintain live, suspended execution state between calls, which is exactly what enables lazy, on-demand production of values (one at a time, only when actually asked for) instead of a function needing to compute and hand back everything at once.

assessments.prompt:
```python
nums = [1, 2, 3]
it1 = iter(nums)
it2 = iter(nums)

print(next(it1))
print(next(it1))
print(next(it2))
```
What gets printed, in order?
options: It raises StopIteration on the third call, since nums has already been exhausted by it1
assessments.explanation: `iter(nums)` returns a brand-new, independent iterator object each time it's called -- `it1` and `it2` are two entirely separate iterators over the same underlying list, each tracking its own position. Advancing `it1` twice (getting `1`, then `2`) has no effect whatsoever on `it2`, which starts completely fresh from the beginning of `nums` when it's created and hasn't been advanced at all yet, so its first `next()` call returns `1`. This is exactly why two independent for loops over the same list don't interfere with each other -- each one gets its own iterator via its own call to `iter()`.

assessments.prompt:
```python
gen = (x * 2 for x in range(3))
print(list(gen))
print(list(gen))
```
What gets printed?
options: RuntimeError: generator already executing
assessments.explanation: The first `list(gen)` fully consumes the generator, pulling every value until it's exhausted, producing `[0, 2, 4]`. A generator has no way to 'rewind' or reset itself -- once it's exhausted (its underlying code has run to completion and raised `StopIteration`), every subsequent attempt to pull a value from it, including a second `list(gen)`, immediately hits that same exhausted state and produces nothing at all: an empty list. This is exactly the tradeoff mentioned for generators versus list comprehensions -- a list can be iterated over as many times as you like, but a generator can only be consumed once, in one pass.

concepts.title: Context Managers
concepts.description: The with statement guarantees cleanup code runs even when an exception occurs, by relying on an object's __enter__/__exit__ methods -- the same guarantee try/finally provides, expressed more concisely and reusably.
learningObjectives: Explain what the with statement does and how it relates to __enter__ and __exit__.
Explain why with guarantees cleanup even when an exception is raised inside its block.
Connect the with statement's guarantee to try/finally, and explain why with is usually the cleaner choice.
Write a simple custom context manager using contextlib.contextmanager and a generator function.
Identify common real-world use cases for context managers beyond files, such as locks.

sections.heading: The with Statement and the __enter__ / __exit__ Protocol
sections.body:
The `with` statement wraps a block of code with guaranteed setup and teardown logic, delegated to an object that implements the **context manager protocol**: an `__enter__` method (called when the `with` block starts) and an `__exit__` method (called when the block ends -- for any reason at all, including an exception).

```python
class Announcer:
    def __enter__(self):
        print("Entering the block")
        return self   # this becomes the value bound by 'as', if used

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
        print("Exiting the block")
        return False   # False means: don't suppress any exception that occurred

with Announcer() as a:
    print("Inside the block")

# Entering the block
# Inside the block
# Exiting the block
```

`with Announcer() as a:` calls `Announcer().__enter__()` and binds whatever it returns to `a`; when the indented block finishes -- normally or via an exception -- Python calls `__exit__` automatically. `__exit__` receives three arguments describing any exception that occurred (`exc_type`, `exc_value`, `traceback` -- all `None` if the block finished normally), and its return value decides whether that exception should be suppressed (`True`) or allowed to keep propagating (`False`, or nothing, since `None` is falsy) -- suppressing exceptions is a powerful but situational capability, and most context managers correctly return `False`/`None` so they only handle cleanup, not swallow errors.

sections.heading: Why This Matters: Cleanup Even When Things Go Wrong
sections.body:
The entire point of `with` is the guarantee that `__exit__` runs **no matter how the block ends** -- whether it finishes normally, hits a `return`/`break`/`continue` that jumps out early, or raises an exception that propagates all the way through. This matters enormously for resource cleanup: closing a file, releasing a lock, closing a database connection, or committing/rolling back a transaction. Without that guarantee, an exception raised partway through a block could skip right past cleanup code that comes after it:

```python
f = open("data.txt", encoding="utf-8")
data = f.read()
process(data)   # if this raises an exception...
f.close()       # ...this line is never reached -- file stays open
```

If `process(data)` raises, the exception propagates immediately, skipping every line after it in this straight-line code, including `f.close()`. This is precisely the same problem `try/finally` was designed to solve, and `with` is built directly on top of that same guarantee -- `__exit__` runs the way a `finally` block runs, regardless of whether the `try` body succeeded or raised. In fact, `with obj:` is roughly equivalent to writing the setup, then a `try/finally` around the block, with `__exit__` called in the `finally`:

```python
# what 'with obj as x: BODY' is roughly equivalent to:
x = obj.__enter__()
try:
    BODY
finally:
    obj.__exit__(*sys.exc_info())
```

`with` is strictly more concise for this specific, very common pattern -- it packages 'set something up, guarantee it's torn down, regardless of what happens in between' into one reusable object, rather than requiring every caller to remember to write their own `try/finally` correctly, every single time.

sections.heading: contextlib.contextmanager: A Lighter Way to Write One
sections.body:
Writing a full class with `__enter__` and `__exit__` is sometimes more ceremony than a simple context manager needs. The `contextlib.contextmanager` decorator lets you write one using an ordinary generator function instead -- the code before the single `yield` becomes `__enter__`'s logic, the yielded value becomes what `as` binds, and the code after the `yield` (typically inside a `try/finally` of its own) becomes `__exit__`'s logic:

```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def announced_block():
    print("Entering the block")
    try:
        yield "some value"   # execution pauses here for the whole 'with' body
    finally:
        print("Exiting the block")

with announced_block() as value:
    print(f"Inside the block, got: {value}")

# Entering the block
# Inside the block, got: some value
# Exiting the block
```

This relies directly on the generator pause/resume mechanics from the Iterators and Generators concept: the `with` block calls `next()` on the generator once to run everything up to `yield`, treating that as `__enter__`; the `with` block's body then runs; and when the block ends, the `with` machinery resumes the generator (via `.send()` or `.throw()` if an exception occurred), running everything after `yield`, treating that as `__exit__`. Wrapping the post-yield code in `try/finally` (as shown above) is important specifically so that cleanup still runs even if the `with` block itself raises -- the exception gets thrown back into the generator at the point of the `yield`, and `finally` ensures the cleanup code after it still executes before that exception propagates onward.

sections.heading: Common Use Cases: Files, Locks, and Beyond
sections.body:
The single most common context manager you'll encounter is `open()` for files -- `with open("data.txt") as f:` guarantees `f.close()` runs even if reading or processing the file raises an exception midway through (this gets covered in full depth in the File Handling concept). Another everyday use case is **locks**, used for coordinating access to shared resources across threads:

```python
import threading

lock = threading.Lock()

def update_shared_counter():
    with lock:              # acquires the lock on entry
        # ... critical section: only one thread executes this at a time ...
        pass
    # lock is released automatically here, even if the critical section raised
```

`with lock:` calls `lock.acquire()` on entry and guarantees `lock.release()` on exit -- which matters enormously here, because a lock that's acquired but never released due to an unexpected exception would deadlock every other thread waiting on it forever. This is the general shape of what context managers are for: pairing an action that sets something up (opening, acquiring, connecting, starting a timer) with a matching action that must tear it back down, and making that pairing airtight against early returns and exceptions, rather than trusting every call site to remember and get the pairing right by hand.

examples.title: Custom Context Manager as a Class
examples.code:
class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        import time
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
        import time
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self.start
        print(f"Elapsed: {elapsed:.4f} seconds")
        return False   # don't suppress exceptions

with Timer():
    total = sum(range(1_000_000))

print(total)
examples.explanation: __enter__ records the start time and returns self (unused here, since the with statement has no `as` clause, but available if needed). __exit__ computes and prints the elapsed time regardless of what happened inside the block -- if `sum(range(1_000_000))` had raised an exception instead of completing normally, __exit__ would still run and print the elapsed time before that exception continued propagating, precisely because __exit__ is guaranteed to run on the way out of a with block, exception or not. Returning False from __exit__ means any exception that did occur is not swallowed -- it keeps propagating normally after cleanup runs.

examples.title: The Same Timer, Written with contextlib.contextmanager
examples.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager
import time

@contextmanager
def timer():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
        print(f"Elapsed: {elapsed:.4f} seconds")

with timer():
    total = sum(range(1_000_000))

print(total)
examples.explanation: This produces identical behavior to the class-based Timer, with noticeably less code. The lines before yield run as __enter__ would; yield (with nothing after it, since there's no `as` clause used here) pauses the generator for the duration of the with block's body; and the finally block, which runs when the generator is resumed as the with block ends, plays the role of __exit__ -- and specifically because it's wrapped in try/finally, it still runs and prints the elapsed time even if the with block's body raises an exception, since the generator gets that exception thrown back in at the yield point, and finally guarantees the cleanup code after it still executes.

examples.title: with vs a Hand-Written try/finally
examples.code:
def risky_operation():
    raise ValueError("something went wrong")

# Manual try/finally version
lock_held = True
try:
    print("lock acquired (simulated)")
    risky_operation()
finally:
    lock_held = False
    print("lock released (simulated)")

# print("unreachable") -- the ValueError still propagates past this point after finally runs
examples.explanation: Even though risky_operation() raises a ValueError, the finally block still runs -- 'lock released (simulated)' prints -- before the exception continues propagating up and (in this snippet, since it's never caught) crashes the program. This is exactly the guarantee a with statement provides automatically via __exit__, without requiring the caller to write try/finally by hand every time. A real lock object's __enter__/__exit__ methods do precisely this acquire/release pairing internally, which is why `with lock:` is preferred over manually calling lock.acquire() and lock.release() -- it's impossible to forget the release() call, or to place it somewhere an early exception could skip past, since __exit__ is guaranteed to run.

misconceptions.description: with is just a shorter way to write code -- it doesn't provide any guarantee that plain sequential code couldn't also provide if you're careful.
misconceptions.clarification: The entire value of with is a guarantee, not just brevity: __exit__ is called no matter how the block ends -- normally, via an early return/break/continue, or because an exception propagated all the way through it. Plain sequential code has no such guarantee -- a line like f.close() written after some risky operation is simply skipped if that operation raises, since the exception propagates immediately past every subsequent line. Getting the same guarantee without with requires an explicit try/finally, which with effectively packages up and automates via an object's __enter__/__exit__ methods, so every caller gets the guarantee automatically rather than needing to remember to write (and correctly write) their own try/finally each time.

misconceptions.description: A context manager's __exit__ method, if it returns something, always suppresses any exception that occurred inside the with block.
misconceptions.clarification: __exit__'s return value specifically controls this: returning a truthy value (most explicitly True) tells Python to suppress the exception -- the with statement exits normally as if nothing happened, and the exception does not propagate further. Returning a falsy value (False, or simply not returning anything, which defaults to None) means the exception, if there was one, continues propagating after __exit__ finishes its cleanup. The vast majority of context managers should return False/None, since silently swallowing exceptions is rarely correct behavior -- __exit__'s job is normally cleanup, not error handling, and conflating the two is a common source of confusing bugs where errors seem to vanish without a trace.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, including whether the exception message appears?
hints: __exit__ is guaranteed to run when the with block ends for ANY reason, including an exception being raised inside it -- track when exactly that happens relative to the raise.
__exit__ returns False here -- what does that tell Python to do with the ValueError after __exit__ finishes running?
Order the four possible outputs: 'enter', 'inside', 'exit', and 'caught: boom' -- figure out which happens before which.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'enter', then 'inside', then 'exit', then 'caught: boom'. __exit__ runs (printing 'exit') before the ValueError propagates out of the with block; since __exit__ returns False, the exception isn't suppressed, so it continues propagating and gets caught by the outer try/except, printing 'caught: boom' last.
exercises.solutionExplanation: with Guard(): calls __enter__ first, printing 'enter'. The block's body then prints 'inside' and raises ValueError('boom'). Because with guarantees __exit__ runs regardless of how the block ends, __exit__ runs next, printing 'exit', receiving the exception's details as its arguments. __exit__ returns False, which tells Python not to suppress the exception -- so after __exit__ finishes, the ValueError continues propagating exactly as if the with statement weren't there, and it's caught by the surrounding try/except ValueError, printing 'caught: boom'. If __exit__ had returned True instead, the exception would have been suppressed entirely, and 'caught: boom' would never print.

exercises.prompt: Using contextlib.contextmanager, write a context manager function `suppressing(*exception_types)` that suppresses (silently ignores) any exception of the given type(s) raised inside its with block, letting the program continue normally after the with statement -- similar in spirit to contextlib's own suppress(). For example, `with suppressing(ZeroDivisionError): 1 / 0` should not raise.
hints: You'll need a try/except (not just try/finally) around the yield, since you're not just cleaning up -- you're deliberately catching and discarding a specific exception.
Catch the exception with `except exception_types as e:` -- since exception_types is a tuple of types (from *args), except can accept a tuple directly.
Simply catching the exception and doing nothing else in that except block (or a bare `pass`) is enough to suppress it -- you don't need to re-raise it.
exercises.solutionExplanation: suppressing wraps the with block's body (represented by yield) in a try/except targeting exactly the exception types passed in as exception_types (a tuple, thanks to *args). If the with block raises one of those types, the generator's except clause catches it right at the yield point (since a with block's exception gets thrown back into the generator there), and doing nothing in the except body (pass) means the exception is simply discarded -- it never propagates further, so execution continues normally right after the with statement. Note this deliberately does NOT use try/finally the way the earlier timer example did: finally would let cleanup code run but would still allow the exception to keep propagating afterward, whereas try/except followed by no re-raise is what actually suppresses it. An exception type not listed in exception_types would not match the except clause and would propagate normally, exactly as intended.

assessments.prompt: What is the with statement's core guarantee, compared to writing the equivalent setup/teardown logic as plain sequential code?
options: with only guarantees cleanup runs if the block completes without raising any exception.
with guarantees the context manager's __exit__ method runs when the block ends, whether it completes normally, exits early, or raises an exception -- the same guarantee try/finally provides.
with is purely a stylistic convenience with no behavioral guarantee beyond what plain sequential code already provides.
with guarantees that any exception raised inside the block will always be suppressed automatically.
assessments.explanation: The defining feature of with is that __exit__ is guaranteed to run no matter how the block ends -- including when an exception propagates through it -- which is exactly the guarantee a try/finally block provides, just packaged into a reusable object's protocol instead of requiring hand-written try/finally at every call site. Option A has the guarantee backwards (it specifically covers the exception case, not just the success case). Option C understates it -- plain sequential code has no such guarantee, since an exception skips all subsequent lines. Option D is wrong -- whether an exception is suppressed depends entirely on __exit__'s return value, and most context managers deliberately do not suppress exceptions.

assessments.prompt: Explain how contextlib.contextmanager turns a generator function into a context manager, and why the code after yield is typically wrapped in a try/finally.
assessments.modelAnswer: contextlib.contextmanager lets you define a context manager using a generator function that yields exactly once, instead of writing a full class with separate __enter__ and __exit__ methods. When the resulting object is used in a with statement, entering the block resumes the generator up to its yield -- this is effectively __enter__'s job, and whatever value is yielded becomes what an `as` clause binds. The with block's body then executes. When that body finishes (or raises), the with machinery resumes the generator again -- either normally (if the block completed without an exception) or by throwing the exception back into the generator at the exact point of the yield (if the block raised one) -- and whatever code comes after yield plays the role of __exit__. Wrapping that post-yield code in try/finally matters specifically because of the exception case: if the with block's body raises, that exception is thrown into the generator right at the yield, and without a try/finally around it, the cleanup code after yield would simply never run, since the thrown exception would propagate straight out of the generator before reaching it. Putting the cleanup in a finally block guarantees it still executes -- printing a log message, releasing a resource, closing a connection -- before that exception is allowed to continue propagating out of the with statement, mirroring exactly what a hand-written __exit__ method needs to do to honor the with statement's cleanup guarantee.

assessments.prompt:
```python
class Silencer:
    def __enter__(self):
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
        print("exit ran")
        return True

with Silencer():
    print("before")
    raise ValueError("oops")
print("after the with block")
```
What gets printed?
options: before / exit ran / after the with block
before / exit ran, and then the ValueError still propagates and crashes the program
exit ran / before / after the with block
before / exit ran (but the program crashes anyway, since __exit__ can only suppress built-in exceptions, not user-raised ones)
assessments.explanation: "before" prints, then `raise ValueError("oops")` fires. `__exit__` still runs, as guaranteed, printing "exit ran" and receiving the exception's details as its three arguments. Because `__exit__` returns `True` -- a truthy value -- Python suppresses the exception entirely: it does not continue propagating after `__exit__` finishes. Execution then continues normally right after the `with` statement, printing "after the with block". `__exit__` treats every exception type identically for this purpose -- there's no distinction between built-in and user-defined exceptions in how the return value is interpreted.

assessments.prompt:
```python
class Inspector:
    def __enter__(self):
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
        print(exc_type, exc_value)
        return False

with Inspector():
    print("no problems here")
```
What gets printed?
options: no problems here / None None
no problems here -- __exit__ is never actually called at all, since no exception occurred
None None / no problems here
no problems here / <class 'NoneType'> <class 'NoneType'>
assessments.explanation: `__exit__` runs unconditionally when the `with` block ends, whether or not an exception occurred -- that's the entire point of the guarantee. Since the block here completes normally with no exception raised, Python calls `__exit__(None, None, None)`: all three of `exc_type`, `exc_value`, and `traceback` are the actual value `None` (not the class `NoneType`), specifically documenting 'nothing went wrong.' So after "no problems here" prints from inside the block, `__exit__` runs and prints `None None`.

assessments.prompt:
```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def broken_context():
    print("setup")
    yield
    print("teardown")   # NOT wrapped in try/finally

with broken_context():
    print("body")
    raise ValueError("bad")
```
What happens?
options: setup / body print, then the ValueError propagates uncaught -- "teardown" never prints, since there's no try/finally to run it before the thrown-back exception exits the generator
setup / body / teardown, and then the ValueError propagates
setup / teardown / body, with no error at all
The program hangs, because a generator with no try/finally around yield cannot be resumed after an exception
assessments.explanation: "setup" prints, then `yield` pauses the generator for the with block's body. "body" prints, then the `raise ValueError("bad")` fires -- and because the block raised, the `with` machinery resumes the generator by throwing that exception back in at the exact point of `yield`. With no `try/finally` (or `try/except`) wrapped around the `yield`, the generator has nothing to catch it with, so the exception propagates straight out of the generator function immediately -- `print("teardown")`, sitting after the unprotected `yield`, is simply never reached. This is exactly why the lesson's own examples wrap the post-yield cleanup code in `try/finally`: without it, an exception in the with block's body silently skips the cleanup entirely.

concepts.title: Type Hints
concepts.description: Type hints document expected argument and return types for humans, IDEs, and static checkers like mypy, but Python itself never enforces them at runtime -- a real and common source of surprise for developers coming from statically-typed languages.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of type hints: documentation, IDE support, and enabling static checkers like mypy.
State precisely why type hints are not enforced at runtime, and predict what happens when code violates its own hints.
Write basic type hints for variables and function signatures.
Use Optional/Union (or the X | None syntax) to express a value that may be one of several types or may be absent.
Explain gradual typing and why a codebase can mix hinted and unhinted code.

sections.heading: Why Type Hints Exist
The Critical Point: Type Hints Are Not Enforced at Runtime
sections.body:
This is worth stating as directly as possible, because it surprises developers coming from Java, C#, TypeScript, or any language where type declarations are checked and enforced by the compiler or runtime: **Python itself does absolutely nothing with type hints at runtime.** They are not checked, not validated, not enforced in any way by the interpreter. Code that blatantly violates its own type hints runs without complaint:

```python
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

print(add("hello", "world"))   # 'helloworld' -- runs fine! No TypeError, no warning.
print(add(2, 3))                # 5
```

`add("hello", "world")` violates the hint `a: int, b: int` outright -- and Python runs it anyway, because `+` happens to also work on strings, concatenating them. The hints exist purely as **metadata**, stored on the function object (inspectable via `add.__annotations__`) for tools to read -- Python's own runtime behavior is completely unaffected by their presence. Catching this kind of mistake requires *actually running* a separate static type checker like `mypy` as a deliberate step in your workflow (locally, or in CI) -- it will not happen automatically just because you wrote the hints. This is precisely why type hints are often summarized as 'a contract enforced by tooling and discipline, not by the language' -- writing accurate hints and then never running a checker against them gives you the *appearance* of type safety with none of the actual guarantee.

sections.heading: Basic Syntax for Variables and Functions
sections.body:
Variable annotations use a colon: `age: int = 30`, or even without an initial value, `age: int` (which just records the intended type without creating the variable at all -- referencing `age` before assigning it would still raise `NameError`, exactly as it would with no annotation). Function signatures annotate each parameter the same way, and the return type is written after `->`:

```python
name: str = "Amy"
scores: list = [85, 90, 78]         # a bare 'list' says 'a list of something', unspecified
tagged_scores: list[int] = [85, 90, 78]   # more precise: specifically a list of ints

def average(numbers: list[int]) -> float:
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)
```

`list[int]` (using square brackets directly on the built-in `list`, valid since Python 3.9) is more informative than a bare `list`, since it also documents what the list is expected to contain. Before 3.9, the equivalent required importing `List` from the `typing` module (`from typing import List; List[int]`) -- you may still see that older style in codebases that need to support earlier Python versions, but modern code can use the built-ins directly.

sections.heading: Optional and Union: Expressing 'Could Be One of Several Types'
sections.body:
Many real values can legitimately be one of several types, most commonly 'this type, or `None`.' `Optional[X]` (from the `typing` module) means exactly `Union[X, None]` -- 'an `X`, or `None`.' `Union[X, Y]` more generally means 'an `X` or a `Y`.' Modern Python (3.10+) supports a more concise, built-in syntax using `|` directly, which most new code now prefers:

```python
from typing import Optional, Union

def find_user(user_id: int) -> Optional[str]:      # returns a str, or None if not found
    ...

def find_user_modern(user_id: int) -> str | None:    # equivalent, Python 3.10+ syntax
    ...

def parse_id(raw: Union[str, int]) -> int:           # accepts either a str or an int
    return int(raw)

def parse_id_modern(raw: str | int) -> int:          # equivalent, Python 3.10+ syntax
    return int(raw)
```

A function hinted to return `Optional[str]` (or `str | None`) is explicitly documenting -- and letting a type checker verify -- that callers must handle the `None` case; code that does `find_user(5).upper()` without checking for `None` first is exactly the kind of mistake a static checker like mypy is designed to flag, even though (per the point above) Python itself would only raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` at runtime, and only on the specific occasions the function actually returns `None`.

sections.heading: Gradual Typing: You Don't Have to Hint Everything
sections.body:
Python's type hint system is explicitly designed around **gradual typing**: you can add hints to some functions and variables while leaving others completely unhinted, and mix both freely within the same file, module, or codebase. An unhinted parameter or variable is implicitly treated (by checkers like mypy) as `Any` -- a type that's compatible with everything and triggers no type-checking complaints, effectively opting that piece of code out of static checking rather than being an error.

This matters practically in a few ways: you can incrementally add hints to an existing, large, unhinted codebase function-by-function or module-by-module, rather than needing an all-or-nothing rewrite; quick scripts and prototypes can skip hints entirely without any tooling complaint, and add them later if the code graduates into something more permanent; and third-party libraries without their own hints (or with incomplete ones) don't block you from hinting *your own* code that uses them, since the boundary just falls back to `Any` there. This flexibility is a deliberate design choice distinguishing Python's approach from languages where typing is all-or-nothing -- it's part of why type hints have been adopted so widely without requiring a disruptive, one-time migration.

examples.title: Hints Are Metadata, Not Enforcement
examples.code:
def divide(a: int, b: int) -> float:
    return a / b

print(divide(10, 2))        # 5.0 -- matches the hints, works as expected
print(divide("10", "2"))     # TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for /: 'str' and 'str'
print(divide(10.5, 2))       # 5.25 -- a float where int was hinted, runs fine, no complaint at all

print(divide.__annotations__)
# {'a': <class 'int'>, 'b': <class 'int'>, 'return': <class 'float'>}
examples.explanation: divide("10", "2") does raise an error -- but that TypeError comes from the / operator not supporting two strings, not from Python checking the a: int hint and rejecting the call for violating it; Python never looked at the hints at all before running the function body. divide(10.5, 2) shows this even more clearly: it violates the a: int hint (10.5 is a float, not an int) and runs completely fine, producing 5.25, with zero warning or error of any kind, because float division works perfectly well regardless of what the hint says. __annotations__ shows that the hints are simply stored as a dict on the function object -- available for tools to inspect, but never consulted by the interpreter when the function is actually called.

examples.title: Optional and the None-Handling It Documents
examples.explanation: The -> Optional[int] hint documents, for both human readers and a static checker, that this function might return an int OR might return None -- callers are expected to handle both cases. The if result is not None: check does exactly that. The commented-out final line shows what happens if a caller ignores the hint's implication and doesn't check for None: Python raises a TypeError at the point of actually using result2 as if it were guaranteed to be an int, but only when that code path actually runs (here, only when the list has no negative numbers) -- a static checker like mypy would flag `result2 + 1` as an error immediately, without needing to run the code or hit that specific input at all.

examples.title: Gradual Typing: Mixing Hinted and Unhinted Code
examples.explanation: hinted_total has full type hints; unhinted_discount has none at all. Both run identically well -- Python doesn't care either way, since it never enforces hints regardless of whether they're present. A static checker treats unhinted_discount's parameters as the implicit Any type, meaning it won't flag anything about how they're used, effectively opting that function out of type checking without causing an error. This mixture is completely normal in real Python codebases: hints get added where they're most valuable (public APIs, complex logic, anything a team wants a type checker to help enforce) without requiring every single line of a codebase to be hinted before any of it can be checked.

misconceptions.description: If a function has a type hint like def f(x: int), calling it with a string, like f("hello"), will raise a TypeError because Python enforces the hint.
misconceptions.clarification: Python's runtime does not check type hints at all -- calling f("hello") runs the function body exactly as written, using whatever value was actually passed, regardless of what the hint says. If an error occurs, it's because some operation inside the function's body genuinely fails for that type (e.g. trying to do string-specific math that doesn't apply), not because Python compared the argument against the hint and rejected the call. Catching a hint violation before runtime requires actually running a separate static type checker like mypy as a deliberate, explicit step -- it is not something that happens automatically just because hints are present in the code.

misconceptions.description: Once you start using type hints in a project, you have to hint every function, parameter, and variable, or the type checker (and Python itself) will complain.
misconceptions.clarification: Python's type hint system is deliberately designed for gradual typing: hinted and unhinted code can coexist freely, in the same function, file, or codebase, with no requirement to hint everything. Python itself never complains about missing hints under any circumstances, since it doesn't process hints at runtime at all. A static checker like mypy treats any unhinted parameter or variable as the implicit Any type, which is compatible with everything and produces no type-checking errors -- it simply means that particular piece of code is not being type-checked, not that it's wrong. This lets teams add hints incrementally, function by function, rather than needing to hint an entire codebase before gaining any benefit at all.

exercises.prompt: What does this print? Does it raise any error?
exercises.code:
def label(value: int) -> str:
    return f"Value: {value}"

print(label(42))
print(label(3.14))
print(label("already a string"))
hints: None of these three calls match int exactly in every case -- does Python check the hint `value: int` before running the function body?
f-strings can format basically any value into a string representation -- would an f"{value}" ever fail just because value isn't literally an int?
Trace what f"Value: {value}" produces for each of the three different types of argument actually passed in.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'Value: 42', 'Value: 3.14', 'Value: already a string' -- all three print successfully with no error at all. The int hint is never checked or enforced by Python; f-strings can format any value regardless of its type.
exercises.solutionExplanation: value: int is purely a hint -- Python's runtime never checks it before or during the call, so label(3.14) and label("already a string") run exactly like label(42) does, just substituting whatever value was actually passed into the f-string. f"Value: {value}" works for essentially any object (it calls str() on whatever value holds internally), so there's no operation inside the function body that would fail for a float or a string either. All three calls succeed and print, with zero errors or warnings anywhere -- demonstrating directly that the int hint has no runtime effect whatsoever; it exists solely as documentation and as something a separate static type checker like mypy could flag (mypy would indeed report label(3.14) and label("already a string") as type errors, without ever running this code).

exercises.prompt: Write a function `safe_divide(a: float, b: float) -> Optional[float]` that returns the result of a / b, or None if b is zero (avoiding a ZeroDivisionError). Include the type hints exactly as specified, remembering that a return type of Optional[float] means the function can return either a float or None.
hints: You'll need `from typing import Optional` to use Optional in the hint.
Check whether b == 0 before dividing, and return None in that specific case instead of performing the division.
The Optional[float] return hint is just documentation for callers and tools -- it doesn't change how you write the function's actual logic, just what you choose to return in each branch.
exercises.solutionExplanation: safe_divide checks b == 0 first and explicitly returns None in that case, avoiding the ZeroDivisionError that a / b would otherwise raise. In every other case, it returns the ordinary float result of the division. The Optional[float] return hint documents both possible outcomes for anyone reading the signature or using a static checker -- it signals that callers should be prepared to receive None and should check for it (with `is not None`, as in the usage example) before treating the result as a usable float, exactly the same documentation-and-checker-only role type hints play everywhere else, since Python itself does nothing special with this hint at runtime.

assessments.prompt:
```python
def combine(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

result = combine([1, 2], [3, 4])
print(result)
```
What happens when this runs?
options: Python raises a TypeError immediately when combine is called, because [1, 2] and [3, 4] don't match the int hints.
It prints [1, 2, 3, 4], since + concatenates lists, and Python never checks the a: int / b: int hints at runtime.
It raises a TypeError, but only because mypy is silently run automatically whenever a type-hinted function is called.
It raises a SyntaxError, because type hints require their declared types to be enforced at the point of definition.
assessments.explanation: Python's runtime never checks type hints, so calling combine([1, 2], [3, 4]) runs the function body exactly as written, with a and b bound to the actual list arguments passed in. Inside, a + b uses list concatenation (since + is defined for lists), producing [1, 2, 3, 4] -- no error occurs at all, despite blatantly violating the a: int, b: int hints. Option A and C both incorrectly assume some runtime or automatic type-checking occurs -- catching this would require deliberately running a separate tool like mypy as an explicit step, which never happens implicitly. Option D is wrong -- hints don't affect syntax validity in any way tied to enforcement.

assessments.prompt: A junior developer says: 'I added type hints to all my function signatures, so now my code is type-safe.' Explain what's true and what's missing from that statement.
assessments.modelAnswer: It's true that adding type hints is a meaningful, valuable step -- hints document intended types directly in the code, improve IDE autocomplete and inline help, and, crucially, make it possible for a separate static type checker like mypy, pyright, or pyre to analyze the codebase and catch type-related mistakes without ever running it. What's missing is the word 'now': writing the hints themselves does not make the code type-safe by itself, because Python's interpreter does absolutely nothing with type hints at runtime -- it doesn't check them, validate them, or enforce them in any way. A function hinted as def add(a: int, b: int) -> int can be called with completely mismatched types, like strings or lists, and Python will run it without complaint, doing whatever the function's actual code happens to do with those values (which might work by accident, might raise a totally unrelated error, or might produce a silently wrong result). The hints only become an actual safety net once a static type checker is genuinely run against the code -- as a manual step locally, or (much more reliably) wired into CI so it runs on every change -- and its output is actually acted on. Type hints without a checker running against them are documentation with the appearance of a guarantee, not a guarantee itself; the real type-safety benefit comes from the combination of accurate hints AND a checker actually being run and its findings addressed, not from the hints existing in the source code alone.

assessments.prompt:
```python
def transform(value: str, factor: int = 2) -> list:
    return [value] * factor

print(transform.__annotations__)
```
What gets printed?
options: {'value': <class 'str'>, 'factor': <class 'int'>, 'return': <class 'list'>}
{'value': <class 'str'>, 'factor': 2, 'return': <class 'list'>}
{} -- since transform has never actually been called, its annotations haven't been generated yet
{'value': <class 'str'>, 'factor': <class 'int'>} -- with no 'return' key, since return hints aren't stored in __annotations__
assessments.explanation: Type hints are stored as plain metadata on the function object the moment it's defined -- calling the function isn't required for `__annotations__` to exist. The dict maps each hinted parameter name to its annotated type object, and specifically includes a `'return'` key for the `-> list` annotation. Note that the default value `2` for `factor` does not appear in `__annotations__` at all -- only the *type hint* `int` does; defaults are a separate mechanism (visible instead via `__defaults__`) that `__annotations__` has nothing to do with.

assessments.prompt: Which pair of type hints are exactly equivalent in meaning?
options: Optional[str] and Union[str, None]
Optional[str] and Union[str, int]
Union[str, None] and plain str, since None is just treated as a valid str value
Optional[str] and str | int
assessments.explanation: `Optional[X]` is defined to mean exactly `Union[X, None]` -- 'an X, or None' -- so `Optional[str]` and `Union[str, None]` are the identical hint written two different ways. `Union[str, int]` (option B) means 'a str or an int,' with no mention of None at all -- not equivalent. Option C is wrong on two counts: `None` is not a valid `str` value, and dropping it from the hint entirely changes the meaning. Option D pairs `Optional[str]` (str-or-None) against `str | int` (str-or-int), which describes a completely different set of allowed types.

assessments.prompt: A codebase has a function `def calculate(a, b): return a + b` with no type hints at all, sitting alongside several fully type-hinted functions elsewhere in the same file. Which statement is accurate?
options: Python runs calculate() exactly the same way it would run any hinted function -- hints are never enforced either way -- and a static checker like mypy treats calculate's unhinted parameters as the implicit Any type, so it won't flag anything about how they're used
Python raises a SyntaxError, because hinted and unhinted functions cannot coexist in the same file
mypy refuses to check any of the hinted functions in the file until every function in that file has hints
calculate() runs measurably slower than a hinted equivalent, since Python must infer its parameter types at every call
assessments.explanation: Python's gradual typing model means hinted and unhinted code freely coexist, in the same function, file, or codebase, with zero restriction. Python itself never enforces hints on any function regardless of whether they're present, so calculate() runs identically to a hinted version. A static checker like mypy treats an unhinted parameter as the implicit `Any` type -- compatible with everything, and specifically not an error -- which lets teams add hints incrementally without needing an all-or-nothing rewrite before gaining any benefit. There's no runtime performance difference of any kind tied to the presence or absence of hints.
